workflow: In-company customs tariff classification: assigning and defending the HS/HTS/CN commodity code for each SKU or part per destination country, inside importers, exporters, and the brokers who file for them. EVIDENCE LIMITATION, STATED UP FRONT: WebSearch was exhausted (200/200) before this analysis; every regulator, court, audit, association, press and GTM-vendor host (cbp.gov, rulings.cbp.gov, ecfr.gov, gov.uk, taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu, douane.gouv.fr, legifrance, gao.gov, eca.europa.eu, thomsonreuters.com, descartes.com, e2open.com, help.sap.com, developer.avalara.com) was blocked; GitHub search and directory APIs are repo-scoped in this session. Sourced material is therefore limited to (1) a full dated scrape of CBP's CROSS ruling database (216,164 rulings to 2025-03-13), which I recomputed myself, (2) Avalara's open AvaTax SDK models, (3) HMRC's open-source ATaR case-manager source and message strings, and (4) READMEs of hobby classifiers. No in-company classification log, escalation rate, override rate, duplicate-classification share, cost per classification, headcount, misclassification rate or penalty total exists in any reachable source. Legal mechanics (19 CFR 177, 19 USC 1484/1592/1625, UCC Art. 33/34) are recall, unverified.
geography: US (10-digit HTSUS, CBP NY/HQ rulings in CROSS), EU (8-digit CN plus TARIC, Binding Tariff Information under the Union Customs Code, EBTI database), France (RTC issued by DGDDI under the EU regime), UK (Advance Tariff Rulings under TCTA 2018 s.24, HMRC open-source case manager). Multinationals need a code per destination regime, so one product family can carry several parallel settlements.
triggering_event: Company side (recall of industry practice, unverified): a new SKU or part is created in the ERP item master, or a sourcing change moves production to a new country, or a supplier changes composition, or an annual HTS/CN edition renumbers a line, or a broker, port officer or audit challenges a declared code. The item cannot ship or clear until it carries a code per destination; Avalara's item model exposes exactly this state machine: bulk classification jobs with counters classified / inProgress / notClassified / failed / notFound, a review-queue criterion TariffCodeNeedsReview, and per-item hsCodeClassificationStatus with status and details (vendor SDK source, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/avadev/AvaTax-REST-V2-DotNet-SDK/main/src/models/ClassificationDetailsModel.cs, ClassificationCriteriaModel.cs, ItemHSCodeClassificationStatusModel.cs). Regulator side, the parallel trigger is an application (HMRC BTIApplication carries goodName, goodDescription, envisagedCommodityCode, relatedBTIReferences, sampleToBeProvided; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hmrc/binding-tariff-classification/main/app/uk/gov/hmrc/bindingtariffclassification/model/Application.scala, government source code) or a post-clearance challenge (HMRC LiabilityOrder from form C592 with entryNumber, traderCommodityCode versus officerCommodityCode, btiReference, repaymentClaim; same file, and officer messages 'Code entered by trader' / 'Code suggested by officer', https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hmrc/tariff-classification-frontend/main/conf/messages). The C592 path is the sourced proof that broker-or-trader versus officer code disputes are a distinct regulator caseload; its volume is unknown.
available_rules: Harmonized System nomenclature with the six General Interpretative Rules and legally binding Section and Chapter Notes; the national extension (HTSUS 10-digit, CN 8-digit, TARIC 10-digit); HS Explanatory Notes and (EU) CN Explanatory Notes; Commission classification regulations binding on all EU authorities and traders (mechanism recalled, volumes unverified); published rulings: CROSS (216,164 dated rulings, 179,080 NY and 37,084 HQ, own computation from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/justinmoonjeli/CROSSFetch/main/cbp_rulings_data.csv, open-source scrape of the CBP API), EBTI (blocked), UK ATaR public search refreshed daily from the case manager (https://github.com/hmrc/binding-tariff-ruling-frontend, government source code); court decisions (CIT/CAFC, CJEU, UK tribunals, recall); plus, in the US since 2018, a chapter 99 overlay of trade-remedy provisions whose applicability turns on the underlying classification and origin. Company-level rules: the company's own item master codes, family templates and any rulings it holds. Legal effect (recall, unverified): a US ruling binds CBP only for the holder and the goods described (19 CFR 177); an EU BTI binds all Member State authorities and the holder for three years and must be cited on the declaration (UCC Art. 33); an HMRC ATaR is 'valid from {0} to {1}' for the holder and third parties are only told 'it can help to provide a ruling if there is already a ruling for goods that are similar, even if the ruling was made in another country' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hmrc/binding-tariff-trader-frontend/main/conf/messages.en, government source code). None of these rules determines the code for a new product without a factual finding; the GIRs are a procedure, not a lookup.
available_facts: Product facts: description, material composition, function, form, construction, packaging, whether presented as a set, and country of origin. Sourced incumbent capture: Avalara ItemModel carries description, itemGroup, category, upc, summary, a classifications list (productCode, systemCode, country, isPremium), a parameters list where each ItemParameterModel has name, value, unit and a boolean isNeededForClassification, customParameters, tags, createdUserId/createdDate/modifiedUserId/modifiedDate, source/sourceEntityId, and an image (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/avadev/AvaTax-REST-V2-DotNet-SDK/main/src/models/ItemModel.cs and ItemParameterModel.cs, vendor SDK source). ClassificationParameterUsageMapModel defines system parameters per tax type group with visibility recommended/optional/mandatory, attributeType Product/Transaction/Calculated, dataType, values and helpText (ClassificationParameterUsageMapModel.cs). So the incumbent already holds structured product facts flagged as classification inputs. Fact availability is the binding constraint at the low-value tail: HMRC's parcel classifier works from free-text descriptions only (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/trade-tariff/trade-tariff-lambdas-fpo-search/main/README.md, government source code), the only HMRC referral reasons are REQUEST_SAMPLE and REQUEST_MORE_INFO (ReferralReason.scala) and a reject reason NO_INFO_FROM_TRADER exists (RejectReason.scala). Hobby classifier authors report that roughly half of mined CROSS labels cite stale statistical suffixes and that chapter 98/99 provisions 'depend on import circumstances, not product text' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vladswork23/us-hts-classifier/main/README.md, open-source project), which is a sourced statement that the facts needed for the trade-remedy overlay are transactional (origin, importer, use), not catalogue attributes.
why_it_escalates: Four sourced or structurally grounded reasons. (1) Missing facts (A): spec sheets absent or vague; the regulator's escalation vocabulary is entirely evidence requests. (2) Factual classification of the specific product against a class that is already settled (B): in 2023-24, 98.0% of CBP rulings with codes fell on a 6-digit line that already had a ruling and 92.2% on a 10-digit line that already had one (chapters 98/99 excluded; own computation from the CROSSFetch CSV), and 9505.90.6000 (festive articles) alone received 168 rulings in two years, each a fresh officer decision on a specific product. (3) Genuine interpretive questions (C): GIR 3(b) essential character for sets and kits (168 of 3,971 rulings in 2023-24 have set/kit in the subject, 4%), parts versus accessories, chapter-note exclusions, and, dominating current US demand, whether a product falls inside a chapter 99 trade-remedy provision or exclusion and what its origin is after multi-country processing: 1,211 of 3,971 rulings in 2023-24 (30%) cite a 9903 code, up from 0% in 2017 and 7% in 2018; 768 (19%) have origin in the subject; 1,730 (44%) mention China (own computation, same CSV). (4) Conflict of authorities (D): NY versus HQ (HQ does 99.1% of the 2,792 superseding rulings), broker versus importer, Member State versus Member State (EU divergence resolved by classification regulation, recall). The decision escalates inside a company when the analyst cannot map the product to an existing family with confidence, when duty stakes are high (a 25-point chapter 99 differential on a high-volume line), or when a challenge arrives; the stakes, not ambiguity alone, drive escalation.
who_resolves: Inside the company: the classification analyst, then a senior classification specialist or the trade compliance manager or director, who does hold company-level rule-making power (can mandate the code for all like SKUs and set the classification procedure); beyond that, a licensed customs broker, outside trade counsel, or the authority through a ruling request (CBP NY rulings, HQ for novel or conflicting questions; HMRC 'within 30 working days ... can take up to 120 days, as per UK law', messages.en; EU BTI 120 days, recall). Only the authority's decision is legally binding, and only for the holder and the described goods (recall). The company-level decision is an interpretation of risk under the reasonable-care (US, 19 USC 1484, recall) or declarant-accuracy (EU UCC Art. 15, recall) standard, not law. Brokers: a licensed broker resolves at entry when the importer supplies no code, which is where importer-broker disputes originate (recall of practice; the HMRC C592 liability case is the sourced regulator-side analogue).
what_gets_settled: Three layers. (1) The code for this item in this country, stored in the item master with dates and user (Avalara ClassificationModel per systemCode and country; ItemHSCodeClassificationStatusModel with createdUserId, modifiedUserId, completedAt) and, on Avalara's premium tier, a free-text 'Justification why this HsCode is attached to this item' with createdDate, createdUserId and country (ItemPremiumClassificationOutputModel.cs, vendor SDK source). (2) A family reading: 'our string lights are electric garlands of 9405, not lamps', 'this bracket is a part of heading X', 'this kit's essential character is the tool'. This is the H-shaped object. Sourced absence: no Avalara model carries a rule predicate over attributes, the GIR or note applied, the authority cited, the deciding role, or an applicability scope; only itemGroup and category (free grouping strings) exist. Whether ONESOURCE Global Classification, Descartes CustomsInfo, SAP GTS or Oracle GTM hold such an object could not be verified (all blocked; recall says they hold classification databases with rationale text and approval workflow, unverified). (3) The regulator's settlement: a ruling with commodity code, effective dates, justification, goods description, searches performed, commercial denomination and exclusions (HMRC Decision.scala, government source code), typed invalidation reasons (INVALIDATED_CODE_CHANGE, INVALIDATED_EU_MEASURE, INVALIDATED_NATIONAL_MEASURE, INVALIDATED_WRONG_CLASSIFICATION; CancelReason.scala), and an appeal ladder (ADR, REVIEW, APPEAL_TIER_1, APPEAL_TIER_2, COURT_OF_APPEALS, SUPREME_COURT; AppealType.scala). Layer 3 is the reference implementation of the mechanism, already built by the owner.
prospective: Yes at every layer, with sourced and recalled limits. Item level: the stored code is applied to every subsequent shipment of that item until changed; Avalara TaxRuleModel is effective-dated (effectiveDate, endDate) and user-stamped (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/avadev/AvaTax-REST-V2-DotNet-SDK/main/src/models/TaxRuleModel.cs, vendor SDK source). Family level: applied prospectively by practice inside the team, but as an untyped convention; no sourced evidence of a versioned family-rule object in any inspected incumbent. Regulator level: a ruling binds the authority for the holder for the described goods (3 years EU, recall); everyone-binding prospective change happens only through HQ modification or revocation: 3,044 of 216,164 rulings (1.4%) were ever modified or revoked, 2,792 superseding rulings of which 99.1% are HQ, and the superseding stream now runs at 29 (2022), 27 (2023) and 31 (2024) per year (own computation, CROSSFetch CSV). Third parties may cite rulings persuasively (20.9% of all rulings, 45,172, cite a prior ruling) but cannot rely on them. So prospective settlement is real but narrow: for the holder's item, or for everyone at roughly 30 nationwide events a year in the US.
recurrence: Sourced at the regulator, unknown inside companies. Across the whole US public loop, classes recur heavily: in 2023-24, 87 six-digit lines account for half of all non-chapter-99 code mentions (1,006 distinct lines); 98.0% of rulings land on an already-ruled 6-digit line and 92.2% on an already-ruled 10-digit line; yet 62% of the 1,512 distinct 10-digit lines seen in 2023-24 appear only once in those two years, and the corpus is 29,994 knit-apparel and 23,565 woven-apparel documents of 259,288 usable (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OrlandoWhite88/qwen36-cpt-customs/main/README.md, open-source project), a concentration that reflects per-garment fibre and construction fact-finding, not repeated interpretive disputes. Same-day clusters of rulings for one product family citing the same precedent (for example four grip-tool rulings on 2024-08-20 all citing ruling 556449) number only 11 groups covering 41 rulings in 2023-24 (own computation), showing that even a family is ruled item by item. Company-level recurrence (share of a team's escalations that are 'same family as something we already decided') is not measurable from public data; the prior from the regulator pattern and from IPSA (93% coverage at coarse class, 37% at fine class) is that recurrence is high at the level the team already governs with family templates and low where escalations actually arise. The one recurrence that demonstrably compounds and changes is the chapter 99 overlay (30% of 2023-24 rulings), which is transaction-fact driven and re-litigated with every tariff action.
current_systems: ERP item master (SAP material master foreign-trade data, Oracle, Dynamics; recall) holding the commodity code per country; Global Trade Management suites: SAP GTS, Oracle GTM, Thomson Reuters ONESOURCE Global Trade and Global Classification, Descartes CustomsInfo, E2open Global Knowledge, Avalara cross-border item classification and Classification MCP server (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/avadev/mcp/main/README.md, vendor documentation), 3CE (recall). Only Avalara's data model was inspected: it stores what was decided (code per system and country), who and when, structured product parameters flagged isNeededForClassification, a bulk-job review queue, an item-level status with details, tax-code recommendations with rank, and a free-text premium justification. Broker systems (CargoWise, Descartes, ABI filers; recall) classify at entry. Precedent lookup: CROSS, EBTI, HMRC ATaR search, plus commercial scrapers (an Apify actor advertises 'ruling status tracking' and 'relationship chains' for 'trade compliance professionals handling hundreds of product classifications', https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HumbleIgnite/cbp-customs-rulings/main/README.md, vendor marketing, weak). Rationale storage in practice: attachments, spreadsheets, SharePoint, email (recall, unverified). LLM classifiers grounded in CROSS: 73.0/59.6/44.9/38.2/32.6% at 2/4/6/8/10 digits on 89 held-out rulings with gpt-5-mini, author warning that one run is 'insufficient for trustworthy conclusions' and that 'CROSS labels are not ground truth' (vladswork23 README, open-source, anecdotal); a competitor accuracy claim of 92-96% at 6 digits is unattributed (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ShantanuTaro/HS-Code-Lookup-for-Customs/main/README.md, individual claim, weak).
minimal_product: WOULD DO: a classification settlement register sitting beside the item master and GTM, not replacing them. For each escalated decision it records a typed settlement: the deciding facts as structured attributes (reusing the GTM's own parameter vocabulary), the rule reading (GIR step, section/chapter note or exclusion applied), the authority relied on (CROSS/EBTI/ATaR ruling number, classification regulation, court case, or the company's own held ruling), the decider and their authority level (analyst, senior specialist, compliance director, broker, counsel, customs authority), effective dates, and an applicability predicate that turns the family reading into a rule ('attributes X, Y, Z in country C => code K'). New SKUs are matched on attributes to existing settlements; when facts match, the code and its rationale are proposed or applied deterministically and written back to the GTM/ERP; when they do not, the case is routed to the owner with the nearest settlements shown. It versions settlements and invalidates them on typed triggers, mirroring HMRC's CancelReason enum: annual HTS/CN renumbering, an HQ modification or revocation notice (a watchable stream of about 30 per year in the US), a new EU classification regulation, a new held ruling. It exports the audit trail a CBP Focused Assessment or EU/French post-clearance audit asks for (recall). WOULD NOT DO: classify from scratch (that is Avalara/3CE/ONESOURCE content and LLM classifiers, and it is B work); extract facts from spec sheets or chase suppliers (A work, the largest bucket); decide chapter 99 applicability or origin from transactional facts it does not hold; file ruling requests; make any settlement legally binding; own the item master or replace the GTM; serve brokers as a cross-client precedent pool without a licensed broker's supervision of each entry (recall of 19 CFR 111 supervision duty, unverified). Honest framing: everything in WOULD DO is a set of fields and a matching rule on the incumbent's item and classification objects, which is why the verifier and the H5-H8 falsification cluster both read it as a feature (H6).
buyer: Head or Director of Global Trade Compliance, or Customs Manager, at importers and exporters with several thousand active SKUs across two or more customs regimes; secondarily, classification-service leads at customs brokers and 3PLs who classify for many clients. Budget exists but is already committed to GTM licences, content subscriptions and broker fees, all of which are unverified in size (vendor and association hosts blocked). The buyer is identifiable and has company-level rule-making power (a point in favour under section 2), but the same buyer's obvious first move is to ask the GTM vendor for rationale and family-rule fields, and Avalara already sells a per-item justification as a premium feature.
roi_logic: All inputs are estimates unless marked; no company-side number could be sourced. Labour case, one mid-size importer: new SKUs classified per year 5,000 (estimate); share escalated beyond the analyst 10%, so 500 cases (estimate); analyst plus senior time per escalated case 2 hours (estimate); H share of escalations 5-15% (verifier's corrected range, estimate), so 25-75 cases per year are repeats of a settled family; time saved per such case 1.5 hours (estimate); loaded cost 60 USD per hour (estimate). Saving: 25 to 75 cases x 1.5 h x 60 USD = 2,250 to 6,750 USD per year. At ten times the SKU flow (50,000 new SKUs) it is 22,500 to 67,500 USD per year, still below a plausible standalone ACV once integration to the item master is priced. Labour alone cannot carry a product. Error-cost case: exposure = annual import value of a mis-set family x duty differential x years open (US liquidation and 1592 look-back, recall) plus penalties (negligence up to 2x the duty loss, recall, unverified). Example: a family importing 10 million USD per year mis-set across a 5-point differential = 500,000 USD per year; across a 25-point chapter 99 differential = 2.5 million USD per year. This is where value lives, but it requires two unsourced premises: that inconsistent classification of like items is a material failure mode at companies that already run like-item search in a GTM, and that a rationale-and-family-rule register, rather than a better classifier, review sampling or a ruling request, is what prevents it. No misclassification rate, penalty total or audit finding rate was reachable (GAO, ECA, CBP compliance measurement all blocked). Conclusion: ROI is plausible only for high-duty, high-volume families at large importers, which is precisely the population that already buys GTM suites and rulings; for everyone else the arithmetic fails.
review_split_A_to_H: Estimates for the in-company escalation queue, basis stated; no measurement exists. A missing evidence 20-30% (basis: HMRC's only referral reasons are REQUEST_SAMPLE and REQUEST_MORE_INFO and a NO_INFO_FROM_TRADER reject reason exists, government source code; HMRC's parcel classifier is description-only). B factual classification 35-45% (basis: 92.2% of 2023-24 CBP rulings fall on an already-ruled 10-digit line yet each is a fresh per-product decision; apparel chapters, the largest corpus share, turn on fibre and construction facts). C interpretation of an existing rule 15-25%, of which most is chapter 99 applicability and origin after multi-country processing (30% and 19% of 2023-24 rulings respectively) plus GIR 3(b) sets and kits (4%) and parts questions. D conflict of authorities 3-5% (basis: NY versus HQ supersession is 1.4% of the corpus; broker-importer and Member-State divergence add an unmeasured margin). E true discretion and F negotiation under 2% (classification is not discretionary or negotiated; broker fee disputes aside). G one-off under 5%. H repeatable ambiguity settleable prospectively 5-15% of escalations (the verifier's corrected range; basis: family-level recurrence is visible in the public corpus, but the part that is H, a company reading of essential character or note scope for a family, is normally frozen into the item master and family templates already, so the unmet residual is the rationale record). Note that most SKU classifications never escalate at all; H as a share of all classification decisions is smaller still.

penalties_triggered: Main bottleneck is missing data rather than interpretation: partly triggered. The regulator's only escalation reasons are evidence requests, its parcel classifier is description-bound, and hobby classifiers find chapter 99 outcomes depend on transaction facts absent from product text; in-company A plus B is estimated at 55-75% of escalations.

Existing systems already solve the problem adequately: substantially triggered. Avalara (the only inspected incumbent) stores the code per country, dates, users, structured classification parameters, a review queue, ranked recommendations and a free-text justification; HMRC's open-source case manager implements the entire loop for the regulator. The residual is a family-rule and authority-provenance object, a field-level gap (H6), not a missing system.

Value per decision too small: triggered on labour. 25-75 H-type repeats per year at a mid-size importer are worth low single-digit thousands of dollars; only error avoidance on high-duty families is material, and that premise is unsourced.

Decision volume too low: triggered at the H level. Nationwide everyone-binding settlements run at about 30 HQ supersessions per year in the US; company-level H is a small slice of escalations, which are a small slice of classifications.

Implementation requires replacing or deeply writing into a core system of record: partly triggered. The code lives in the ERP item master and GTM; a register that does not write back is shelfware, and one that does is a GTM feature.

Humans must remain involved for legal or commercial reasons: partly triggered. No statute mandates a human per classification, but the importer or declarant remains liable under reasonable-care and accuracy standards and a company settlement is never legally binding, so a reviewer signs off on high-duty families regardless of precedent (recall, unverified).
Buyer unclear: not triggered. The trade compliance director is identifiable, though their budget is captured by GTM and broker spend.
Decisions discretionary, one-off, or ambiguity rarely repeats: not triggered. Classification is rule-bound and classes demonstrably recur at 6- and 10-digit level.
Regulations prohibit automation: not triggered in US, EU or France.
regulatory_constraints_US_EU_FR: All of this section is recall, unverified, because every legal host was blocked. US: the importer of record must exercise reasonable care in classification (19 USC 1484) and is liable for duty loss plus penalties under 19 USC 1592 (negligence, gross negligence, fraud tiers), mitigated by prior disclosure; binding rulings under 19 CFR 177 bind CBP for the holder and the described transaction only, and modification or revocation of a ruling or an established treatment requires notice and comment (19 USC 1625(c)), which is why the sourced HQ supersession stream is small and public; licensed customs brokers (19 CFR 111) must exercise responsible supervision over entries they file; since 2018 the chapter 99 overlay (Section 301, 232, and later actions) attaches large duty differentials to classification and origin, which the CROSS data show now drives about 30% of rulings. No rule requires a human per classification decision; automation of internal classification is unregulated. EU: Union Customs Code (Reg. 952/2013) Art. 15 makes the declarant responsible for accuracy; Art. 33 BTI decisions bind all Member State customs authorities and the holder for three years and must be invoked on declarations; Art. 34 governs invalidation when the CN, explanatory notes, a classification regulation or a court judgment changes; Commission classification regulations adopted through the Customs Code Committee bind everyone; penalties are national (Art. 42). EBTI is public. The EU AI Act's Annex III lists border-control and migration uses by public authorities, not commercial tariff classification, so a company-side classification register is not a high-risk system; GDPR is not engaged by goods data. France: the DGDDI issues RTC through the SOPRANO online service under the UCC regime; sanctions for misdeclaration sit in the Code des douanes (Art. 412 and 414 series); the ESSOC 2018 right-to-error regime softens first-offence negligence penalties for good-faith declarants; declarations run through DELTA. Differences that matter to the product: EU/French BTIs are broader in legal effect (all authorities, must be used, publicly searchable) so the external precedent corpus is more authoritative there than in the US, while the US has the larger and more volatile chapter 99 problem. None of the three jurisdictions mandates a human in the loop after a settlement exists, which is the one section 2 criterion the workflow clearly passes.
verdict: Weak evidence; the thesis fails for a standalone product in this workflow, and the workflow survives only as the single cheapest place to run the brief's base-rate experiment. Sourced facts that favour it: the outcome is a code; a 216,164-ruling dated public precedent corpus with supersession links exists; classes recur heavily (98% at 6 digits, 92% at 10 digits in 2023-24); an owner with company-level rule-making power exists; no jurisdiction mandates a human per decision; the inspected incumbent stores the code, dates, users, parameters and a free-text justification but no family rule, rule reading, or authority provenance. Sourced facts that defeat it: the regulator that owns the loop re-decides every product by hand even when the class is settled, which is the brief's penalty pattern, not its target; everyone-binding prospective settlements number about 30 per year in the US; 30% of current US rulings are chapter 99 applicability questions driven by transaction facts, not catalogue attributes; the only inspected incumbent's data model is one field-set away from closing the gap; and no in-company escalation, recurrence, cost or error number exists anywhere reachable, so the H share of 5-15% is an estimate resting on structure. Labour ROI is a few thousand dollars per year per mid-size importer; only unsourced error-avoidance on high-duty families could carry a price, and that population already buys GTM suites and rulings. Kill or continue: obtain one importer's or broker's classification escalation log (200-500 cases) and code it into the brief's eight categories; continue only if categories 7 and 8 together exceed roughly 20% of escalations at more than about 1,000 escalations per year, and if the settled family readings are found to live outside the GTM (spreadsheets, email, broker files) rather than in it. The prior from every reachable source is that both conditions fail, and that the correct owner of the residual object is the GTM item master, not a new product. Evidence limitation restated: no regulator, vendor, court or industry statistic was reachable; all numbers above are computed from GitHub-hosted primary artefacts, labelled estimates, or labelled recall.
